summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to plan, lead and check marking-out work in general engineering and fabrication. You will read drawings, datums and tolerances, choose and check the right tools for the accuracy needed, work out hole circles, angles, diagonals and allowances, and mark out plate, bar, angle and pipe. You will also make and prove templates for repeat parts, check other people's marking, and keep the records that let every part be traced.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). **Marking out** (also called marking off or laying out) means transferring the sizes and shapes on a drawing onto the material, as lines, centres and punch marks, so that it can be cut, drilled, bent, machined or welded in the right place. Every later step follows your lines. An error made at the marking table is cut, drilled and welded into the job, and it is usually found only when the part will not fit.

At Level 3 you do more than mark a line. You **plan** the job, choose a method that suits the tolerance, check the tools, do the calculations, lead a small team, check other people's work and keep the records. This unit covers general engineering work: plates, brackets, flanges, bar, angle, tube and pipe. Large structural members, roof trusses and sheet-metal developments are covered in the unit Mark off/out structural fabrications and shapes (MEMCOR0092B).
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and fabricators, fitters and machinists who lead marking-out work in a workshop.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Work safely at the marking table
Handle plate and sections safely, use punches and scribers without injury, keep marking fluids away from heat, and keep the area lit and tidy.
Read the drawing and plan the job
Check the revision, sizes, tolerances, datums and notes; check the material; plan the order of work and who does what.
Choose and check the tools
Match the method to the tolerance; check squares, rules, height gauges and dividers before a big job; take faulty tools out of use.
Do the calculations
Work out hole positions on pitch circles, coordinates, diagonals, angles, pitches and allowances, and check them by a second method.
Mark out accurately
Set up datums and centre lines; mark lines, arcs, holes, slots and outlines on plate, bar, angle and pipe; punch accurately.
Use templates for repeat parts
Make, prove, label and control a template, and check the parts marked from it.
Check, record and report
Have marked parts checked against the drawing, fill in the inspection sheet, label and store parts, and report errors.
Lead the team
Brief the team, share the work, guide trainees, and hand over clearly at the end of a shift.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on drawings, datums, tolerances, tools, calculations, marking methods, templates, checking, safety and records.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms and calculated sizes) and longer answers in full sentences, such as planning a team job, setting up datums, or choosing a method for a tolerance.

**Two team practicals**: planning, marking out and inspecting a flange plate with bolt holes on a pitch circle (worked out by two methods); and making and proving a template, then marking a batch of gussets and angle cleats and proving a large rectangle square by its diagonals. The assessor watches your plan, your calculations, your checks and records, your part in the team, your PPE and how you leave the area.

blocks.note: Short answers ask for exact names: height gauge, angle plate, gauge block, vernier, template, pitch, machining allowance, tapped hole, slot. Learn the Key terms in the Revision section, and practise the calculations until you can do them without the notes.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Safe working at the marking table

blocks.p: Marking out looks like quiet work, but the hazards are real: heavy plate, sharp edges and burrs, pointed tools, chips flying off punches, flammable marking fluid, and long bars sticking out into walkways. As a team leader you plan these controls before the work starts.

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Lifting and moving plate and sections
Back injury; fingers and feet crushed when a plate slips, tips or drops onto the table.
Plan the lift before you touch the steel
Use a crane, hoist, plate clamp, trolley or a planned team lift with one person calling the moves
Safety boots and gloves
Lower plate gently onto the table; never let it drop or slide
Sharp edges and burrs
Deep cuts to hands and arms from sheared, sawn and flame-cut edges.
Deburr edges before marking
Gloves when handling
Carry sheet by its edges with gloves, never by sliding it through your hands
Scribers, dividers and trammels
Stab wounds and scratches; points left on the bench catch hands.
Cap the point or stick it in a cork when not in use
Carry points down; never carry them in a pocket
Store in a rack or case
Punching
Chips of hardened steel fly off a mushroomed punch head or a chipped hammer face; a missed blow hits the fingers.
Safety glasses whenever anyone is punching
Grind mushroomed heads back; replace cracked punches
Hammer head tight on its handle, face not chipped
Hold the punch near its lower end, fingers clear of the head
Marking fluids and solvents
Most marking blue is alcohol-based: its vapour can catch fire from a spark or flame. The fumes and the liquid can irritate eyes, skin and lungs.
Read the safety data sheet (SDS)
Use small amounts; keep the lid on
Good ventilation; no smoking
Well away from welding, cutting and grinding sparks
Used rags in a closed metal bin
Long material
People trip over or walk into bars and pipes that stick out; material rolls or falls off the table.
Support long pieces on trestles or stands
Chock round bar and pipe
Flag the ends that stick out; keep walkways clear
Poor lighting
Scales and lines are misread; people trip.
Good, even light over the marking table
A portable lamp for dark corners
Clean safety glasses

blocks.note: Marking blue dries fast because the solvent evaporates, and the vapour is heavier than air: it collects low down and near the bench. Never blue a part next to a welding bay, a grinder or a hot plate, and let it dry before anyone strikes an arc near it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Caring for the surface plate and marking table

ul: Lower work gently onto a surface plate and lift it off; never slide heavy work across it. Knocks and wear spoil the flat reference surface that every height is measured from.
Never hammer, punch or file on a surface plate. Punch on the marking table or on a steel block.
Wipe the plate and the base of every tool clean before use: a grain of grit under a height gauge puts every line out.
Cover the plate when it is not in use. A cast-iron plate is wiped with a thin film of light oil to stop rust; a granite plate is kept clean and dry.
Do not use the surface plate as a shelf for tools, drawings or cups.

blocks.p: Steel grows as it warms: about **0.012 mm per metre for every 1 °C**. A 2 m plate that has been standing in the sun at 55 °C is about 0.6 mm longer than it will be at 30 °C in the shop (2 × 0.012 × 25 = 0.6 mm). For general work this does not matter. For close work, let the plate cool in the shade to the same temperature as your tools before you mark it.

blocks.note: In Jamaica's heat, plate stored outside can be too hot to handle by midday, marking fluid evaporates faster from open tins, and sweat makes gloves slippery on smooth plate. Bring plate into the shade early, keep tins closed, and change damp gloves before handling heavy or sharp material.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Before you mark: check the drawing and the material

flow: Check the drawing number and **revision** against the job card and the drawing register; if they do not agree, stop and ask the supervisor
Read the title block: material, thickness, quantity, scale, projection, units and the general tolerance
Read every note: finish, hole types, edge preparation, items marked after welding
Find the **datums** the designer used, and check that the sizes add up to the overall sizes
Check the material supplied: grade, thickness and size, with room for the part and its allowances
Write down any query and get an answer before anyone marks or cuts

blocks.note: If the drawing seems wrong, do not 'correct' it yourself. Raise a written query with the supervisor or drawing office. A change agreed by phone should be written on the drawing, signed and dated by the person who agreed it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **datum** is the edge, line, face or point that sizes are measured from. The designer chooses datums that matter for fit: the edge that sits against another part, the centre of a bore, the face that bolts down. Mark from the **same datums as the drawing**, so the features end up where the designer meant them.

head: Datum
When you use it
How you set it up
rows: Two true edges at 90°
Rectangular plates with sawn, guillotined or machined edges
Check each edge straight with a straight edge and square to the other with a square; mark them 'datum'.
Scribed datum lines
Plates with rough flame-cut or sheared edges
Scribe a straight line just inside the rough edge with a straight edge (or the height gauge on a surface plate), then a second line at 90°, checked with a large square or by 3-4-5.
Centre lines
Round or symmetrical parts: flanges, discs, symmetrical brackets
Scribe two centre lines at 90° through the centre; measure every feature from them.
The surface plate
Three-dimensional work: brackets, blocks, bar
The plate is the datum for heights; the height gauge measures every height from it.

blocks.p: **Measure every size from the datum**, not from the last mark. Measuring from mark to mark (chain measuring) adds the small error of each reading to the next. If eight holes are each set out 0.2 mm long from the one before, the last hole is 1.6 mm out. Measured from the datum, each hole is out by no more than one reading error.

No part can be made to an exact size, so the drawing gives a **tolerance**: how far the real size may be from the drawn size and still be accepted. The two limits are the largest and smallest sizes allowed.

head: How it is written
What it means
Limits
rows: Up to 0.25 mm either way
Up to 0.3 mm over, nothing under
General tolerance note, for example '±0.5 unless stated'
Applies to every size that has no tolerance of its own
Size ± 0.5
A tolerance written on a size
Overrides the general note for that size
As written on the size

blocks.h: Match the method to the tolerance

blocks.p: Choose a method that is accurate enough for the tolerance, but no slower than it needs to be. Tight work is spoiled by rough methods, and time is wasted using fine methods on rough work. The figures below are typical; the tools your Centre has and the job decide.

head: Tolerance (typical)
Suitable method
Checks
rows: About ±1 mm or more (cut lines on bar, sheet and long members)
Tape or rule, square, scribed or soapstone line; chalk line on long work
Re-measure from the same end; check the line is square on every face.
About ±0.5 mm (bolt holes in base plates and brackets)
Steel rule, combination square, dividers and scriber from datum edges; light punch, check, then final punch
Check pitches, the diagonals of the hole pattern and the edge distances before final punching.
About ±0.2 to ±0.25 mm
Vernier or digital height gauge on a surface plate, with angle plate or vee blocks; vernier caliper to check
Check with a caliper; a second person checks.
Tighter than about ±0.1 mm
Marking is only a guide: final positions are set on the machine (readout or CNC) or by a drilling jig
First-off check with a measuring instrument; record it.

head: Allowance
Why it is needed
Typical amount (follow the drawing and supervisor)
rows: Machining allowance
Flame-cut edges are rough and hardened by the heat; extra metal is left outside the finished line so it can be machined off.
A few millimetres per edge, often about 2 to 5 mm.
Saw cut (kerf)
Each cut turns the width of the blade or disc into chips or sparks.
About 1 to 2 mm for a band saw; about 3 mm for an abrasive cut-off disc; more for flame cutting.
Squaring the end
Mill ends of bar, tube and pipe are often not square or are damaged.
A few millimetres trimmed off before the first part is measured.
Weld shrinkage
Welds shrink as they cool and pull parts out of position.
Holes that must line up after welding are often marked and drilled after welding, or the drawing gives an allowance.

blocks.p: Always mark which side of a cut line is **waste**, for example with a few strokes of soapstone or the word WASTE, so the cutter keeps the line on the part.

ul: A **clearance hole** is slightly bigger than the bolt so it passes through easily, for example 11 mm for an M10 bolt. Structural bolts commonly have holes 2 mm bigger than the bolt up to M24 and 3 mm bigger above that; the drawing and the design code decide.
A **tapped hole** has a thread cut inside it. It is first drilled with a **tapping drill** a little smaller than the thread, then tapped.

A **slot** is a hole made longer in one direction so the part can be adjusted. The centres of its two end radii are (overall length − width) apart. A slot 18 mm wide and 60 mm long has its centres 42 mm apart, with a radius of 9 mm at each end.

head: Thread (ISO metric coarse)
Tapping drill (usual)
Clearance hole (medium fit)
rows: M6
5.0 mm
6.6 mm
M8
6.8 mm
9 mm
8.5 mm
11 mm
22 mm

blocks.note: These are the usual figures from tapping-drill and clearance-hole charts. Use the drawing's size first, then your Centre's chart. Mark a tapped hole's centre exactly like any other; the circle you scribe round it is the tapping-drill size.

Use
Points to watch
rows: Steel rule (150 to 1000 mm)
Measuring, setting dividers and calipers
Read with your eye square to the scale to avoid parallax. If the end is worn, measure from the 10 mm line and add 10 mm to the reading.
Steel tape
Long sizes
Use the same tape for the whole job; support it and pull it steadily.
Vernier, dial or digital caliper
Checking hole centres, edge distances and small sizes
Close the jaws and check the zero first.
Vernier, dial or digital height gauge
Scribing lines at an exact height above the surface plate, and measuring heights
A vernier usually reads to 0.02 mm, a digital gauge to 0.01 mm. Zero it on the clean plate; keep the scriber sharp and tight.
Surface gauge (scribing block)
Scribing lines at a height set from a rule
Quicker but less accurate than a height gauge.
Gauge blocks (slip gauges)
Hardened steel blocks of exact size for checking height gauges and calipers
Keep them clean and oiled; never drop them.

head: Tool
Use
Points to watch
rows: Scriber
Fine lines on steel
Hardened or carbide point; lean the point into the corner between the straight edge and the work so the line runs tight against the edge.
Engineer's try square
Lines at 90° to a true edge
Stock held firmly against the datum edge.

Lock nuts tight; still read by eye, so it suits general work.

Good on thin sheet and for many repeat marks.

Must be the same diameter as the hole.

head: Equipment
Use

A flat reference surface: the datum for every height
Angle plate

An L-shaped cast-iron block with two faces at 90°; work is clamped to it so a face stands square to the surface plate. Turning the angle plate on its side lets you mark the second direction from the same set-up.
Vee blocks (a matched pair) and clamps
Hold round bar and pipe so they cannot roll; the centre of the bar is then at a known height
Parallels, packing and screw jacks
Raise and level work on the surface plate

Marks lines along the centre of round bar and pipe

Best on
Notes

Shows lines on a dark, rough surface.

blocks.h: Checking your tools before a big job

blocks.p: At Level 3 you make sure the tools are accurate **before** the team starts. One bad square or worn rule can spoil a whole batch.

head: Tool
How to check it
rows: Square
Compare it with the Centre's master square, or

Flip test: hold the stock against a true straight edge and scribe along the blade; turn the square over and scribe again from the same point. If the two lines do not lie on top of each other, the square is out by **half** the gap.
Height gauge
Clean the base and the plate
Check the zero on the surface plate
Set it on a gauge block (or a stack, for example 50 mm and 100 mm) and check the reading
Scriber sharp and tight
Steel rule and tape
End not worn, bent or burred
Compare with a reference rule or tape; tapes from different makers can differ by a millimetre or more over 10 m
A tape hook that slides a little is normal: it moves by its own thickness so pull and push readings both start at zero
Dividers and trammels
Points sharp and equal; joint firm; set them from the rule, scribe an arc, and measure it again.
Calipers
Close the jaws and check zero; check on a gauge block.
Punches and hammers
Points ground to the right angle; heads not mushroomed; hammer head tight.

blocks.p: Write the date and the result of each check in the **tool record**. The record shows the tool can be trusted, and if a fault is found later, it shows which jobs the tool was used on. A tool that fails is taken out of use at once, tagged 'DO NOT USE' with the fault, and reported to the supervisor or store keeper. Do not bend or file it yourself. A tool that has been dropped is checked before it is used again.

blocks.note: Flip test example: after turning a 300 mm square over, the two lines are 0.6 mm apart at the end of the blade. The square is 0.3 mm out over 300 mm, which is 1 mm over a metre: too much for marking bolt holes.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: On a 0.02 mm vernier, read the whole millimetres on the main scale up to the vernier's zero, then find the vernier line that lines up exactly with a main-scale line and multiply its number of divisions by 0.02 mm. Example: the zero is just past 47 mm and the 14th small division lines up: 47 + (14 × 0.02) = **47.28 mm**. Read square on, in good light.

At Level 3 you work out positions; you do not guess them or find them by trial. Write every calculation on the plan sheet, round to 0.1 mm for marking, and check each result by a second method or a second person.

blocks.note: Before any angle calculation, check your calculator shows DEG (degrees), not RAD or GRAD. In radian mode, sin 30° comes out as about −0.99 instead of 0.5, and every position will be wrong.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the long side (the hypotenuse) equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: **c² = a² + b²**. You use it to prove a rectangle square, to find the straight-line distance from a datum corner to a hole, and to check a hole pattern.

ul: Rectangle 900 mm × 400 mm: diagonal = √(900² + 400²) = √(810 000 + 160 000) = √970 000 = **984.9 mm**. Both diagonals must be equal; if they are not, the shape is a parallelogram and the corners are not square.

The **3-4-5 rule**: a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 (or 6, 8, 10 or any multiple) has a right angle between the two shorter sides. To set out a square corner on a big sheet, mark 600 mm along one line and 800 mm along the other; when the distance between the two marks is exactly 1000 mm, the corner is 90°.

blocks.p: The **pitch circle diameter (PCD)** is the diameter of the circle through the hole centres. With n holes equally spaced, the centres are **360° ÷ n** apart, measured from the middle. There are two ways to mark them.

**Method 1: stepping off.** The straight-line distance (chord) between neighbouring centres is **chord = PCD × sin(180° ÷ n)**. Scribe the pitch circle, mark the first centre where a centre line crosses it, set the dividers to the chord and step round.

head: Number of holes (n)
Angle between centres
Chord factor sin(180° ÷ n)
rows: 0.5000 (chord = radius)

ul: Example: 5 holes on a 160 mm PCD: chord = 160 × 0.5878 = **94.0 mm**.

Stepping off can add up small errors. The last step must land exactly on the first centre. If it misses, divide the miss by the number of steps and change the divider setting by that amount: a miss of 1.2 mm over 8 steps means changing the setting by 0.15 mm. Then step round again from the start.
Do not confuse the chord with the distance round the arc. The arc between centres (PCD × π ÷ n) is always a little longer than the chord.

blocks.p: **Method 2: coordinates.** Each centre is found from the two centre lines: **x = R × cos θ** across and **y = R × sin θ** up, where R is the pitch circle radius and θ is the angle of the hole from the horizontal centre line. The height gauge or a rule from the centre lines then marks each one.

Example: 8 holes on a 240 mm PCD (R = 120 mm), straddling both centre lines, so the holes are at 22.5°, 67.5°, 112.5° and so on. x = 120 × cos 22.5° = 120 × 0.9239 = **110.9 mm**; y = 120 × sin 22.5° = 120 × 0.3827 = **45.9 mm**. So four holes are at 110.9 mm and 45.9 mm from the centre lines, and the other four at 45.9 mm and 110.9 mm. Check: the chord = 240 × 0.3827 = 91.8 mm, and the two holes at ±45.9 mm on the same side are 91.8 mm apart, as they should be.

blocks.note: Pipe flanges usually have their bolt holes **straddling** the centre lines (no hole on a centre line), so that two flanges on the same pipe line up and the valves and fittings sit square. Always check which way the drawing places the first hole.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Angles with sin, cos and tan

blocks.p: In a right-angled triangle with angle θ: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse; cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse; tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.

ul: A line at 20° from a datum edge, over a run of 250 mm along the edge: offset = 250 × tan 20° = 250 × 0.364 = **91.0 mm** from the edge.
A line 300 mm long at 25° to the edge: its far end is 300 × sin 25° = 300 × 0.423 = **126.8 mm** from the edge, and 300 × cos 25° = 271.9 mm along it.
To find an angle from two sizes, use the inverse key: a line rising 60 mm over 200 mm is at tan⁻¹(60 ÷ 200) = 16.7° to the edge.
Number of holes in a row = (distance between the end holes ÷ pitch) + 1. A 690 mm bar with the end holes 45 mm from each end and a 60 mm pitch: (690 − 90) ÷ 60 = 10 spaces, so **11 holes**.
Pitch = distance between the end holes ÷ number of spaces. 7 holes over 540 mm between end holes: 540 ÷ 6 = **90 mm**.
Slot centres = overall length − width (see the Drawings section).

blocks.p: Length of bar used = (number of parts × part length) + (number of cuts × kerf) + any end trim. Example: 7 parts of 240 mm, a 2 mm saw kerf and 5 mm to square the mill end: (7 × 240) + (7 × 2) + 5 = 1680 + 14 + 5 = **1699 mm**.

blocks.note: Check every result a second way: a coordinate answer against the chord, a pitch against the overall length, a diagonal against 3-4-5. Write both on the plan sheet so the checker can follow your working.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Deburr the edges and clean the area to be marked: wire-brush loose scale and rust, wipe off oil and grease.
Put on a thin, even coat of the right marking medium and let it dry. A thick coat flakes and hides the line.
Lay the part on a clean, flat table or surface plate, supported so it cannot rock.

flow: Check the drawing, the material and the tools
Prepare and coat the surface
Set up the datums (true edges or scribed datum lines)
Scribe the centre lines
Mark the centres of holes and arcs with a light prick punch
Scribe circles and arcs, then the straight lines that join them (tangent lines are drawn after the arcs)
Check every centre and line against the drawing
Final punching: centre punch for holes, light witness marks along cut lines
Scribe guide circles round hole centres
Write the part mark, job number and waste side; have a second person check

ul: **Parallel to a true edge:** odd-leg calipers run along the edge (quick and good to about ±0.5 mm on long edges); the combination square used as a depth gauge; or the height gauge on a surface plate for the best accuracy.
**Square to an edge:** a try square or combination square from a true edge. On large sheets, use 3-4-5 or intersecting arcs.
**Long straight lines:** a straight edge; on rough work, a chalk line held tight and snapped.
**Bisecting a line:** with the dividers set to more than half the line, strike arcs from both ends above and below; the line through the crossings cuts it in half at 90°.

**Finding the centre of a circle or arc:** mark three points on it, join them with two chords, and bisect each chord. The two bisectors cross at the centre. This is how you find the centre of a rough flame-cut disc.

flow: Make a light mark with the prick punch exactly where the lines cross
Look at it closely, with a magnifier if needed, and check it against the drawing
If it is off, lean the punch towards the true position and tap to draw the mark over, then stand the punch upright and punch again
When it is right, deepen it with the centre punch, held upright
Scribe a guide circle the size of the hole round it, and for larger holes a second, smaller circle

ul: **Guide (proof) circles** show the driller whether the drill has drifted off centre, and show the checker afterwards whether the hole is in the right place.

**Witness marks** are light punch marks along a cut line, close together on curves and further apart on straight lines. After cutting, half of each mark should still show on the edge, which proves the cut followed the line.
On thin sheet, punch lightly on a flat steel block so the sheet does not dent or distort.
Never punch on the surface plate.
**Height gauge:** zero it on the plate, set the height, lock it, and scribe with a light, steady stroke, keeping the base flat on the plate.

**Angle plate:** clamp the work to the angle plate so the face to be marked stands square to the surface plate. Mark the lines in one direction with the height gauge, then turn the angle plate onto its side to mark the lines at 90° from the same set-up.

**Vee blocks:** a round bar laid in a matched pair of vee blocks has its centre at a known height. Measure the height of the top of the bar and subtract half the diameter. Example: a 40 mm bar whose top is 92.00 mm above the plate has its centre at 72.00 mm. A flat 5 mm deep is scribed at 87.00 mm.
Turn the bar a quarter turn, check the first line is upright with a square, and scribe again to make a cross on the end face that shows the centre.

blocks.note: If you zero the height gauge on anything other than the surface plate (for example on top of a parallel), every height you set is measured from that surface, not from the plate. Write down where you zeroed, or zero on the plate itself.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Flat bar centre line:** set odd-leg calipers to about half the width and scribe from each edge in turn; the true centre is midway between the two lines. Adjust until the lines meet.
**Round bar end:** use the centre head of the combination set: scribe a line, turn the bar, scribe again; the lines cross at the centre.

**Angle:** the **back mark** is the distance from the heel (the outside corner) to the line of hole centres, measured on the outside face of the leg. The drawing or a back-mark table gives it. Mark it with a combination square used as a depth gauge, or odd-leg calipers run from the heel, then mark the pitches along it from a datum end.
**Square lines round a section:** square across each face from the same datum face and check that the lines meet at the corners.

**A line along a pipe**, parallel to its centre line: lay a straight length of angle along the pipe, with the pipe sitting in the angle's inside corner, and scribe along the angle's edge. A box square or pipe centre finder does the same job on shorter work.

**Quarter lines:** the distance round the outside between quarter lines is the outside diameter × π ÷ 4. Use the actual outside diameter, not the nominal bore: 100 mm nominal bore pipe is 114.3 mm outside diameter, so its quarter lines are 114.3 × 3.142 ÷ 4 = 89.8 mm apart round the outside.

**A square cut line round a pipe:** wrap a flexible strip with straight, parallel edges (thin sheet, plastic or heavy paper) tightly round the pipe so its edges meet and line up with no step, then scribe or mark along its edge.

Mark the **centre line** and outline of brackets, stiffeners and lugs on the part they will be welded to, with the side they go on clearly shown. The welder can set them in place, and the checker can see after welding whether they have moved.

Holes that must line up with parts already fixed, such as bolts cast into a client's concrete base, are often marked and drilled **after welding**, because weld shrinkage moves parts. Otherwise a drilling jig holds the positions.

**Stainless steel faces on show:** do not scribe or punch them; the mark stays. Use a fine marker or pencil, and use tools that are used only on stainless steel, as carbon-steel particles left on the surface rust.
**Aluminium and thin sheet:** do not scribe across bend lines; the scratch can start a crack when the sheet is bent. Use a pencil or marker for bend lines.
**Galvanised and painted material:** a scribed line breaks the coating and will rust. Use a paint marker, and punch only where a hole will be drilled.

blocks.note: In humid coastal air, bright steel that has been cleaned and marked starts to rust within days, and scribed lines through a coating rust along their length. Mark close to the time of cutting, store marked parts under cover, and protect stainless and galvanised surfaces from scratches.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: When many identical parts are needed, a **template** (an accurate pattern checked against the drawing) saves time and makes every part the same. But a template copies its own errors into every part, so it must be made carefully, proved, labelled and controlled.

head: Template material
Good for
Limits
rows: Thin steel sheet (about 1 to 2 mm)
Batches of parts with holes; long life
Heavier; needs cutting and filing
Aluminium sheet
Large, lighter templates
Edges and holes wear faster
Hardboard, plywood or plastic
Large shapes; site templates such as anchor-bolt patterns
Swells or warps with damp; edges wear
Card or paper
One-off shapes, trials, checking a pattern
Tears, stretches and goes soft in damp; not for batches

flow: Mark it out from the drawing, using the drawing's datums
Cut it and file it exactly to the line; remove all burrs
Drill the hole positions small, to suit a transfer punch or a prick punch
Check every size against the drawing: outline, hole centres, diagonals and angles
Have it checked and signed off by the supervisor or assessor before use
Label it: job number, part mark, drawing number and revision, FACE SIDE and the datum edges
Record it and keep it in its set place

ul: Clamp it to the plate against a datum edge or scribed datum lines, so it cannot move.
Scribe round the outline with the scriber held tight against the template edge.
Mark each hole centre with a transfer punch, or with a prick punch through the small pilot hole; then remove the template and finish the centres as usual.
Check a few key sizes on the plate before you mark the next one.
Part-mark each plate as you go, so marked parts are never mixed up.
One template, one job. Do not use a template from an old job because the part 'looks the same'.
If the drawing is revised, the template is checked against the new revision and changed or replaced; the old one is withdrawn.
Check it for wear part way through a large batch: worn edges and enlarged holes make parts drift out of size.
Keep the face side marked. Turning a template over makes a mirror-image part. Do this only when the drawing asks for an opposite-hand part, and then label which face gives which hand.
**First-off check:** the first part marked from the template is fully checked against the drawing before the rest are marked.
**Sample checks:** then every fifth or tenth part, or as the job card says, and the template itself part way through.
Record each check on the inspection sheet: part, size checked, result, checker, date.

blocks.note: Never use the first part cut as a template for the rest. Cutting errors, heat distortion and burrs on that part are copied, and each copy adds its own error.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Checking, records and leading the team

flow: Read the drawing and job card; raise queries
List every part with its quantity on a part list
Check the material and the tools; book the surface plate and height gauge
Choose the method for each tolerance; decide on templates for repeat parts
Share the work: preparing and blueing, marking, checking, recording
Brief the team: the drawing, datums, method, checks and safety
First-off check, then checks during the job
Label, record and store the parts; hand over or report

blocks.p: Give each person a part list and have them tick off each part as it is marked and checked. Then no part is marked twice or missed, and you can see the progress at a glance.

ul: A **second person**, not the marker, checks every marked part against the **drawing** (not against the marker's notes) before any cutting or drilling.

Check: the right datums; every size measured from the datum; hole centres and sizes; pitches and chords; the diagonals of hole patterns and rectangles; edge distances; the outline and waste side; part marks; the quantity.
Record each check on the **inspection sheet**: the drawing size and tolerance, the size measured, pass or fail, the tool used, the checker's name and the date.

**Wrong marks on a part not yet cut:** cancel them so they cannot be mistaken (for example cross them out clearly with a paint marker), re-mark from the correct datum, and have the part checked again.
**Wrong punch marks** cannot be rubbed out. If a wrong centre is close to a right one, the drill may wander into it; the supervisor decides whether the part can be used.
**A batch error:** stop the batch, quarantine and label the parts, find out how far they have gone (marked, cut or drilled), find the cause, and report.

head: Report on a fault should give
Why it matters
rows: Job number, drawing number and revision, part marks and how many parts
So the supervisor knows exactly which parts are affected
What was found, how and by whom
So the finding can be trusted and checked
How far the parts have gone (marked, cut, drilled)
This decides whether they can be re-marked or must be scrapped
The likely cause (wrong datum, worn tool, misread drawing)
So the same mistake is not made again
What has been done already, and the next steps
So nobody repeats the work or uses the parts by mistake
Date, time and your name
So the record is complete for quality checks

blocks.p: A **handover note** at the end of a shift says which parts are marked and checked, which are marked but not checked, which are not started, any tools that are faulty or booked, and any queries waiting for an answer.

ul: Label each part with the job number and part mark.
Store plates flat on bearers, under cover and off the floor, so they stay flat and dry and the marks are not rubbed off.
Log what is stored and where, so the cutting team can find it.

blocks.p: When a trainee makes a mistake, such as measuring each hole from the one before, stop them early, show them the right way (from the datum) and explain why. Let them try again while you watch, then check their work. Praise good work; correct mistakes privately and calmly.

blocks.note: At Level 3 the rule is: mark once, have it checked by someone else, then cut. A mistake found at the marking table costs a few minutes; the same mistake found after drilling costs the plate.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can name the hazards of marking out and say how to control each one, including lifting plate and using marking fluid.
I can care for a surface plate and explain why work is never slid or punched on it.
I can check a drawing's revision, title block, notes and datums before marking, and raise a query.
I can explain what a datum is and set up datums on a plate with rough edges.
I can read a tolerance, give its limits, and say which tolerance applies when a size has its own.
I can choose a marking method that suits the tolerance.
I can name the main marking-out tools and say what each is for.
I can check a square, a height gauge, a rule and dividers, and say what to do with a tool that fails.
I can read a vernier scale.
I can use Pythagoras and the 3-4-5 rule to prove a rectangle square.
I can work out holes on a pitch circle by stepping off (chord) and by coordinates.
I can use sin, cos and tan to mark lines at an angle.
I can work out pitches, numbers of holes, slot centres and cut allowances.
I can mark lines, arcs, holes and outlines in the right order and punch them accurately.
I can mark out round bar, angle and pipe.
I can make, prove, label and control a template, and check a batch marked from it.
I can check another person's marking and fill in an inspection sheet.
I can write a clear report on a marking error and a handover note.
I can plan a team marking job and guide a trainee.

terms: Angle plate
An L-shaped cast-iron block with two faces at 90°, to which work is clamped on a surface plate
Back mark
On an angle, the distance from the heel to the line of hole centres
Centre punch
A punch with a point of about 90° that makes a mark to start a drill
Chord
The straight-line distance between two points on a circle
Clearance hole
A hole slightly bigger than the bolt that passes through it
Datum
The edge, line, face or point that sizes are measured from
Dividers
A tool with two pointed legs for scribing arcs and stepping off equal distances
First-off check
A full check of the first part before the rest of a batch is made
Gauge block
A hardened steel block of exact size used to check measuring tools
Guide circle
A circle the size of the hole scribed round a centre punch mark
Height gauge
A tool with a vernier, dial or digital scale that scribes lines at an exact height above a surface plate
Kerf
The width of material removed by a saw or cutting process
Machining allowance
Extra material left on a part so it can be machined to its final size
Marking blue
A quick-drying coloured fluid on which scribed lines show clearly
Odd-leg calipers
Calipers with one bent leg, used to scribe lines parallel to an edge
Parallax
A reading error caused by looking at a scale from an angle
Pitch
The distance between the centres of two neighbouring holes
Pitch circle diameter (PCD)
The diameter of the circle on which hole centres lie
Prick punch
A sharp punch for light marks on lines and at centres
Scriber
A hardened, pointed tool for scribing fine lines
Slot
A hole made longer in one direction so a part can be adjusted
Surface plate
A flat cast-iron or granite plate used as the reference for heights
Tapped hole
A hole with a thread cut inside it
Template
An accurate pattern, checked against the drawing, used to mark many parts the same
Tolerance
The amount a size may vary from the drawn size and still be accepted
Transfer punch
A punch the same size as a hole, used to mark its centre on the part below
Vee blocks
Matched blocks with a V-shaped groove that hold round bar and pipe
Vernier
A small sliding scale that lets you read a fraction of a millimetre
Witness marks
Light punch marks along a cut line that prove the cut followed it

c1.title: Pump flanges in Spanish Town
c1.text: Damion leads a team of three at a fabrication shop in Spanish Town, St Catherine. They must mark out six flanges for a water-pumping station from 12 mm mild steel discs. The discs were flame cut to about 290 mm diameter; the edges are rough and each disc is about 2 mm out of round. The finished outside diameter, 280 mm, will be machined later. Each flange has a 120 mm bore and ten 18 mm bolt holes on a 250 mm PCD, with one hole on the vertical centre line. The general tolerance is ±0.5 mm.

c2.title: A machined conveyor bracket in Kingston
c2.text: Kerry-Ann, a Level 3 trainee, is marking out a steel bracket for a conveyor at a bottling plant in Kingston. The bracket is L-shaped, 12 mm thick and machined, except that its left end face still has 2 mm of machining allowance on it, to be faced later. The drawing gives all positions along the bracket from the finished left face. Two M10 tapped holes in the upright face are 85 ± 0.1 mm above the base. She is using a surface plate, an angle plate, a 150 mm try square and a digital height gauge.

c3.title: A sprinkler header in Santa Cruz
c3.text: Odane works for an agricultural engineering shop in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. For a farm's irrigation system he must mark out a sprinkler header from galvanised 100 mm (4 in) nominal bore steel pipe, which is 114.3 mm outside diameter. The header is 3.0 m long. It needs a row of ten 22 mm holes along the top, equally spaced, with the end holes 150 mm from each end, and a second row a quarter of the way round the pipe.

c4.title: Hinge brackets in Morant Bay
c4.text: A shop in Morant Bay, St Thomas, has an order for 36 hinge brackets for security doors, each cut from 8 mm plate with a shaped outline and three 10 mm holes. Shellene, the team leader, finds a steel template made last year for a similar bracket. The current drawing is revision D. The template is stamped 'Rev B', and its 3 mm pilot holes are slightly oval from wear.

c5.title: Holes too close to the edge in Montego Bay
c5.text: In an engineering shop in Montego Bay, St James, Garfield's checker finds that on 4 of 20 marked base plates every hole is about 0.8 mm closer to the left edge than the drawing says; the tolerance is ±0.5 mm. The marker had butted the end of a steel rule against the edge, and the end of that rule is worn and rounded. Two of the four plates have already been drilled.

c6.title: A trough side in Port Maria
c6.text: Sanjay is marking a 1500 mm × 800 mm rectangle on a 2440 mm × 1220 mm steel sheet for the side of a water trough, at a shop in Port Maria, St Mary. The sheet's edges are not square, and the largest square in the shop has a 600 mm blade. The trough maker allows ±1 mm on these sizes.

questions.q: Before scribing the pitch circle, how should Damion find the centre of each rough disc?
o: Measure 145 mm in from the edge nearest him and punch the centre there
Use the point where the cutting torch started and finished the circle
Bisect two chords, then check the 280 mm circle fits all round
Set the dividers to 145 mm and find the centre by eye from the edge
questions.why: A rough, out-of-round edge cannot be measured from. Bisecting two chords finds the true centre; checking that the finished 280 mm circle fits inside the rough edge all round makes sure there is metal to machine everywhere.

questions.q: Stepping off the ten holes on the first flange, the tenth step lands about 2 mm past the starting hole. What should Damion do?
o: Close the dividers by about 0.2 mm and step round again from the start
Close the dividers by about 2 mm and step round again from the start
Leave the last space 2 mm short, since the other nine spaces are correct
Move only the last hole back by 2 mm, then punch all ten of the centres
questions.why: The miss is shared by ten steps, so each step was about 0.2 mm too long. Correcting by the full 2 mm would make the miss just as large the other way, and moving one hole leaves an uneven gap.

questions.q: Damion checks the positions by coordinates. How far is the centre of the hole next to the top hole from the vertical centre line? (sin 36° = 0.588, cos 36° = 0.809)
questions.why: The hole is 36° round from the vertical centre line on a 125 mm radius, so its distance across is 125 × sin 36° = 73.5 mm. 101.1 mm is its height above the horizontal centre line, and 77.3 mm is the chord between holes.

questions.q: Before final punching, which check best shows that the ten centres are evenly spaced?
o: Measure from the rough outside edge to each of the centres
Measure the chord between each pair of neighbouring centres
Check that each light mark sits on the scribed pitch circle
Count the marks and check that there are ten on the circle
questions.why: A mark can sit on the circle and still be in the wrong place round it. Equal chords between neighbours (about 77.3 mm here) prove even spacing; the rough edge is not a datum.

questions.q: Where should Kerry-Ann measure the hole positions along the bracket from?
o: The present left face, exactly as it is now
A line 2 mm in from the present left face
The right-hand end face, measuring back along it
The middle of the bracket, measuring both ways
questions.why: The drawing's datum is the finished left face, which will be 2 mm in from the present face once the allowance is machined off. Marking from the present face would put every hole 2 mm out.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann zeroes the height gauge on top of a 25 mm parallel lying on the surface plate, sets it to read 85.00 mm, and scribes the hole line. The bracket's base sits on the plate. How high above the base is her line?
questions.why: A height gauge measures from wherever it was zeroed. Zeroed on a 25 mm parallel, a reading of 85.00 mm is 110.00 mm above the plate. Zero on the surface plate itself, the datum the bracket stands on.

questions.q: In a flip test of her 150 mm try square, the two lines are 0.4 mm apart at the end of the blade. How far out is the square?
o: 0.2 mm over 150 mm
0.4 mm over 150 mm
0.8 mm over 150 mm
0.1 mm over 150 mm
questions.why: Turning the square over doubles its error, so the gap between the lines is twice the real error. The square should be tagged out of use and reported.

questions.q: What is the pitch of the ten holes along the top of the header?
o: 270 mm
285 mm
300 mm
333 mm
questions.why: The end holes are 3000 − (2 × 150) = 2700 mm apart, and ten holes have nine spaces between them: 2700 ÷ 9 = 300 mm.

questions.q: How far round the outside of the pipe from the top row should the side row be marked?
o: About 78.5 mm
About 57.2 mm
About 179.6 mm
About 89.8 mm
questions.why: A quarter of the way round is the outside diameter × π ÷ 4: 114.3 × 3.142 ÷ 4 = 89.8 mm. Using the nominal 100 mm size gives 78.5 mm, which is wrong; 57.2 mm is the radius and 179.6 mm is half the circumference.

questions.q: How should Odane mark the hole centres on the galvanised surface?
o: Scribe deep lines along the whole length so they stay visible on site
Paint marker for the lines, with a light punch only at each centre
Brush marking blue over the zinc, then scribe the lines into the blue
Soapstone lines only, with no punch marks at any of the hole centres
questions.why: Scribed lines break the zinc coating and rust along their length. A marker shows the lines, and a punch mark is needed only where the drill will remove the metal anyway; without it the drill skids on the curved surface.

questions.q: What should Shellene do with the old template?
o: Withdraw it, and make and prove a new one to revision D
Use it, as long as the brackets look the same as before
Use it, and open the oval pilot holes back out to round
Use it for the outline only, and mark the holes by rule
questions.why: The template was made to an old revision and is worn. Every part marked from it would copy its errors. A new template is checked against the current drawing and signed off before use.

questions.q: The new template has been signed off. Which plan for checking the 36 brackets is best?
o: Check only the last bracket, once all 36 of them have been marked
Check every bracket after they have all been cut out of the plate
Check the first fully, then every sixth part and the template
Check the template at the start, then trust it for every part
questions.why: A first-off check catches set-up errors before the batch is marked; sample checks and a check of the template part way through catch drift and wear. Checking after cutting is too late to save the steel.

questions.q: How should the hole centres be transferred from the template's 3 mm pilot holes?
o: Drill each hole to full size straight through the template into the plate
Scribe round the outline only, and add the three holes by eye later
Prick punch through each pilot hole, then check and centre punch
Spray paint through each pilot hole to leave a dot at the centre
questions.why: The prick punch through the pilot hole puts a light mark exactly at the centre, which is checked and then deepened. Drilling through would wear the template's holes, and paint dots are too large to work to.

questions.q: How could the marker have avoided this error with the same rule?
o: Press the worn end of the rule more firmly against the plate edge
Measure every hole from the right-hand edge of the plate instead
Mark each hole from the hole before it, not the edge
Set the 10 mm line on the edge and add 10 mm to each size
questions.why: A worn rule end is short, so every size measured from it is short by the wear. Starting from a clear graduation, such as the 10 mm line, avoids the worn end. The rule should then be tagged and replaced.

questions.q: What should happen to the two plates that have already been drilled?
o: Elongate the holes so the bolts fit, and send them out
Quarantine and label them, and let the supervisor decide
Weld up the holes and redrill them without telling anyone
Send them out, as 0.8 mm is close enough for base plates
questions.why: Drilled plates outside tolerance need a decision by the supervisor (and sometimes the engineer or customer). Labelling and keeping them apart stops them being used by mistake; hidden repairs are never acceptable.

questions.q: Which tape measurements will set out a true right angle at Sanjay's first corner?
o: 600 mm and 800 mm along the lines, then 1000 mm between the marks
600 mm and 800 mm along the lines, then 1400 mm between the marks
800 mm and 1000 mm along the lines, then 1200 mm between the marks
500 mm and 500 mm along the lines, then 1000 mm between the marks
questions.why: 600, 800 and 1000 are 3, 4 and 5 multiplied by 200, so the corner between the two shorter sides is 90°. The other sets do not form a right-angled triangle.

questions.q: With the rectangle marked, Sanjay's diagonals measure 1702 mm and 1698 mm. What should he do?
o: Find which corner is out, correct it, and re-check
Accept it, because the two diagonals average exactly 1700 mm
Accept it, because each diagonal is within 2 mm of 1700 mm
Shorten the longer side by 4 mm so the diagonals come equal
questions.why: Unequal diagonals mean the shape is a parallelogram, not a rectangle, and 4 mm is far outside ±1 mm. The diagonals of a true 1500 × 800 rectangle are both 1700 mm; the corners are corrected until they match.

questions.q: A trainee's calculator shows sin 30° as −0.988. What is the most likely cause?
o: Its battery is running too low to work it out
It is set to grads instead of degrees
It is set to radians instead of degrees
The angle was keyed in as 3, not 30
questions.why: In radian mode the calculator reads 30 as 30 radians, not 30°, and gives −0.988. In grad mode it would give about 0.454, and sin 3° is 0.052. Check that the display shows DEG before any calculation; sin 30° should be 0.5.

questions.q: A line 300 mm long must run at 25° to a datum edge from one corner. How far from the edge is its far end? (sin 25° = 0.423, cos 25° = 0.906, tan 25° = 0.466)
questions.why: The 300 mm line is the hypotenuse and the distance from the edge is the side opposite the angle, so it is 300 × sin 25° = 126.8 mm. 271.9 mm is the distance along the edge.

questions.q: Why are light witness marks punched along a line that will be flame cut?
o: So the flame follows the punch marks without the cutter guiding it
So the line and the cut can be checked after cutting
So the cut edge comes out hardened and does not need grinding
So the plate does not bend or twist from the heat of the cut
questions.why: Scribed and painted lines burn off or get rubbed away. Half of each witness mark should remain on the cut edge, which shows the cutter followed the line.
